hints: Start by recalling from your infectious diseases list what type of pathogen causes TB and what special waxy-walled genus it belongs to.
walkthrough:
Recall the TB Pathogen**
TB is a bacterial infectious disease. The causative genus has a distinctive lipid-rich waxy cell wall that makes it resistant to staining and to phagocytosis. Its full binomial name is Mycobacterium tuberculosis, with Mycobacterium bovis also accepted as a cause.
Final answer: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (accept Mycobacterium bovis / M. tuberculosis).

hints: Think about what elastin normally allows alveoli to do during breathing in and out.
Now link digestion of elastin by elastase to what will happen to the structure of alveolar walls if they lose that property.
Connect that structural change to gas exchange efficiency and then to why tissues would receive less energy for activity.
walkthrough:
From Elastase to Loss of Elasticity**
Elastin is the stretchy protein in alveolar walls that lets alveoli stretch on inhalation and recoil on exhalation. When phagocytes release the enzyme elastase, it digests and weakens this elastin.

From Weak Walls to Less Surface Area**
Without elastin, alveoli overstretch and cannot recoil. Their thin walls burst and merge, so many small alveoli become one large air sac. This is very similar to emphysema. The total surface area available for gas exchange is greatly reduced.

From Less Gas Exchange to Tiredness**
With less surface area, less oxygen diffuses into the blood per minute. Tissues therefore receive less oxygen for aerobic respiration, so less ATP is released for muscle contraction and other activities. The person feels tired all the time because cells must respire anaerobically or at a lower rate.

Final answer: Elastase breaks down elastin in alveolar walls so alveoli lose elasticity and burst to form fewer, larger air sacs. This reduces surface area for gas exchange, so less oxygen is absorbed into blood, reducing aerobic respiration and ATP supply, causing tiredness.

hints: Start with how TB spreads through the air and which living conditions and population movements keep a reservoir of undiagnosed infection.
Think about what happens to the immune system in HIV infection and why dormant TB can then become active.
Consider why TB is hard to find and hard to cure - dormancy, limited healthcare, and the need for very long treatment courses.
Recall what happens when antibiotics are not finished and how this links to MDR-TB and XDR-TB.
Finish by thinking about prevention - limits of BCG vaccine, herd immunity, and lack of education or access to vaccination programmes.
walkthrough:
Transmission Keeps Spreading**
TB spreads in aerosol droplets when infected people cough or sneeze. Overcrowded housing, poor ventilation, migration and travel from high-TB areas, plus a reservoir of undiagnosed and untreated carriers, make it very hard to break the chain of transmission.

HIV and Weak Immunity**
Infection with HIV causes immunodeficiency. This can activate dormant TB bacteria and also makes people much more susceptible to new TB infection. Intravenous drug use further increases HIV risk, linking the two epidemics.

Difficult Diagnosis and Treatment**
TB bacteria can stay dormant for years with no symptoms, so carriers do not seek help and contact tracing is difficult, especially where access to healthcare is limited. Even when diagnosed, treatment is long term (months) and expensive, so many people do not finish the full course, and access to clinics for treatment may be poor.

Drug Resistance Develops**
Incomplete treatment selects for resistant bacteria. Strains showing multi-drug resistance (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) have evolved, making standard antibiotics ineffective and control much harder. This is a key biological factor.

Vaccination and Education Limits**
The BCG vaccine does not always give effective long-lasting protection, herd immunity is difficult to achieve, and concerns about vaccines reduce uptake. Limited access to vaccination programmes, poor cold-chain stability, poor immune response in immunodeficient people, plus low public and health-worker awareness about TB symptoms and control, all hinder control.

Final answer: Biological: airborne droplet transmission; HIV-induced immunodeficiency activates dormant TB and increases susceptibility; pathogen can remain dormant and symptomless; MDR-TB/XDR-TB drug resistance; BCG vaccine not always effective. Social: overcrowded housing, migration/travel, undiagnosed reservoir, limited access to diagnosis, treatment and vaccination, long expensive treatment with poor compliance, poor contact tracing and low awareness.
